Rosa, I am taking over two accounts from a colleague who is leaving at the end of the month, and both of them are yours in the north.
Which two? And more importantly, do you know who the point of contact is at each one?
I have the names on the contract. One of them is a travel manager whose team books everything, and the other is a director whose name I have never seen in an email.
Then you have half the map. The name on the contract is the person whose signature we need. It is almost never the person you call at eleven at night.
So who do I call at eleven at night?
The analyst who actually runs the account. In that company it is a woman who has been there eleven years and who answers in five minutes, which is more than I can say for the director.
Is that written anywhere?
It is written in a list that I keep myself, because nothing in the onboarding pack has it. Let us go through it together before the handover.

Rosa, it is Beatriz. I am putting together the contact sheet for the regional office and I need three names from you before Friday. First, the person who handles pricing for your biggest accounts. Second, your backup, meaning the colleague who covers for you when you are travelling. And third, and this is the one everybody forgets, the person at the client whom you actually call when something goes wrong at eleven at night. Not the name on the contract. The real one. The sheet that we are building is going to be the thing every new colleague reads in their first week, so please give me people, not departments.

Something I tell every new account manager on their first day. The org chart is not the map of this company. It is a diagram that shows who reports to whom, and that is a much smaller piece of information than people expect. The map you actually need is different. It is the list of people who answer quickly, the people who know things that are not written anywhere, and the two or three people whose approval unblocks everything. That list is not published. You build it yourself, in about a year, and the fastest way to build it is to ask the question nobody likes asking: who is the person I should call about this?

Marcos explains that he is taking over two accounts from a colleague who is leaving. Rosa asks which accounts they are and who the point of contact is at each one. Marcos answers with the names and admits that one of them is only written on the contract. Rosa explains the difference between the name on the contract and the person you actually call at night. Marcos asks her to send him the list she keeps, and Rosa agrees to go through it with him before the handover.
